subject: tech
title: Sorting and Searching
about: Sorting means putting things in order, by size, by color or in ABC order, and searching means finding one thing fast, the way a computer finds a photo by its name or its tag (K2-DA-01); sorting things into piles is also one more way to show the same data (K2-DA-03). The cards ask which word or number comes first, why a sorted toy box beats a jumbled one, how a library keeps its books, and what typing a word in the search box brings back. Read it together: ABC order is new this year, so keep an alphabet strip nearby.
tip: Dump a handful of crayons on the table and sort them two ways, by color and then by length, and time how fast he finds the blue one each time.

cards.q: Putting things in order, like smallest to biggest, has a name. What is it called?
cards.note: Sorting means putting things in order: by size, by color, or in ABC order.

cards.q: Looking for one special thing, like your red sock in a big pile, is called what?
cards.note: Searching means looking for one thing. A computer searches by the name you type.

cards.q: You sort three toy cars from smallest to biggest. Which car goes first?
cards.note: Smallest to biggest means the tiny one leads the line and the big one comes last.

cards.q: You sort your blocks by color. Where does a red block go?
cards.note: Sorting by color puts things that match together. Every red thing goes in the red group.

cards.q: Three words: apple, banana, cat. Which word comes first in ABC order?
cards.note: ABC order follows the alphabet. A comes before B and C, so apple is first.

cards.q: Put these in ABC order: dog, bird, fish. Which word comes first?
cards.note: Look at the first letters: b, d, f. B comes first in the alphabet, so bird is first.

cards.q: Put these in ABC order: dog, bird, fish. Which word comes last?
cards.note: B, then D, then F. F is the farthest along the alphabet, so fish goes last.

cards.q: A computer sorts the pet names Zip, Fluffy and Rover into ABC order. Which name is first?
cards.note: A computer sorts names by their first letter, just like you: F, then R, then Z.

cards.q: Library books sit on shelves by first letter. The C shelf comes right after which shelf?
cards.note: Shelves follow the alphabet too. A, then B, then C, all the way to Z.

cards.q: A library has thousands of books. How does it keep them so you can find one fast?
cards.note: Sorted shelves let you walk right to the book. A big pile would take all day.

cards.q: One toy box is sorted: cars here, blocks there. One is a jumble. Which box is faster to search?
cards.note: Sorting first makes searching fast. That is why computers sort their lists.

cards.q: You type cat in the photo search box. Which pictures show up?
cards.note: Search finds the pictures whose name or tag matches the word you typed.

cards.q: A word you add to a photo, like beach or birthday, has a name. What is it?
cards.note: A tag is a label. One photo can have many tags: beach, summer, Grandma.

cards.q: You tagged every beach photo with the word beach. How do you find them all later?
cards.note: Tags make searching easy. Type the tag and every photo with it shows up.

cards.q: Sort the numbers 9, 4 and 6 from smallest to biggest. Which comes first?
cards.note: Smallest first. 4 is smaller than 6 and 9, so it leads the line.

cards.q: Sort the numbers 3, 8 and 1 from smallest to biggest. Which comes last?
You sort your crayons by color, then sort the same crayons by length. Did the crayons change?
cards.note: Same crayons, two ways to sort them. The data stays the same and only the order changes.

cards.q: You sort crayons into color piles. The red pile is the tallest. Which color do you have most of?
cards.note: Sorting into piles shows your data a new way. The tallest pile is the color you have most of.
